counterexample: k = 3, n = lcm(1,2,3) = 6 (so the hypothesis n >= lcm(1,...,k) holds). Interval [6,9] = {6,7,8,9}; pi(3) = 2, so the theorem claims at least k+1-pi(k) = 4-2 = 2 of these have a prime factor > 3. But 6 = 2*3, 8 = 2^3, 9 = 3^2 all have gpf <= 3, so only 7 qualifies: 1 < 2. The step fails at i = 0: n+0 = 6 has gpf <= p_{pi(k)} yet no prime power p^v | 6 with p^v > 3, because the 'otherwise' inequality only yields n+i <= lcm(1,...,k) <= n, which is not a contradiction when n = lcm and i = 0. Equivalently k = 2, n = 2: [2,4] contains only 3 with a prime factor > 2, while the claim demands 2.
reasoning_summary: Steps 0003-0007 are statement/notation and are fine. Step 0009 asserts: if gpf(n+i) <= p_{pi(k)} then some prime power p_i^{v_i} | n+i with p_i^{v_i} > k, justified in 0010 by 'otherwise n+i <= prod_{p<=k} p^{v_p(k)} = lcm(1,...,k) < n'. The supporting divisibility argument is correct (if every p^{v_p(n+i)} <= k then v_p(n+i) <= v_p(lcm(1,...,k)) for all p <= k, so n+i | lcm(1,...,k) and n+i <= lcm(1,...,k)). But the hypothesis of the theorem in 0005 is only n >= lcm(1,...,k), not n > lcm(1,...,k), so for i = 0 with n = lcm(1,...,k) the conclusion n+i <= lcm(1,...,k) is consistent, not contradictory. Hence the existence claim in 0009 fails precisely at the boundary case, and with it the counting in 0012 (the exceptional set can have pi(k)+1 elements), making the stated theorem false: k = 3, n = 6 and k = 2, n = 2 are explicit counterexamples. The rest of the argument (distinctness of the assigned primes in 0010 via p_i^{min(v_i,v_j)} | i-j with 0 < |i-j| <= k, the Grimm corollary in 0016, and the converse lemma in 0022) is sound, and the closing remark in 0026 implicitly repairs the gap by requiring n+i not to divide lcm(1,...,k); but as written with n >= lcm the proof is invalid at step 0009.
